I've shipped over 300+ PRs the past month using @bot and @claudeai Duet.

Duet feels smarter, Grok Bot gets more done without me.

And i'm struggling to choose which one should be my daily driver..

Grok Bot:

Pros:
> Feels like a true EMPLOYEE: I hand it a task and can come back an hour later with finished work. If I had it a single task it rarely needs me to do anything, and me being a single developer @hirealli this really helps how fast we can iterate and improve our products.
> UI/UX: I've truly never used an app that just feels this easy that is this powerful, everything just.. works.
> Speed / Tone: The responses I get actually feel read-able, there not some essay I need to dig through every response, it also just feels so fast.
> X Integration: How easy it is to just work alongside X.

Cons:
> Usage is terrible: I have the Ultra plan, and am scared to ask it to do simple tasks, routines, etc because I can watch my usage go down by the minute.
> Seems less smart: Almost like its effort level or even the model has been changed recently. It used to seem more smart.
> Cursor Agents: simple fix? Cursor agent. simple UI button on a local app? Cursor agent. I've told it to utilize @t3dotcodes and it is a 50/50 on if it launches a new T3 session or new Cursor Agent.
> Poor Tracking: Its hard to know what my agents are working are, where they are in the work, and most times I end up having to nudge and ask.

Duet:

Pros:
> Best Model: Of course Duet's best feature is that it's powered by Opus 5.5 and its so smart.
> Task Management: Very easy to view all my tasks, what is working, what is stuck needing me, and when its completed
> Claude Ecosystem: How easy it is to navigate and steer my claude code sessions and use the overall claude ecosystem straight from Duet

Cons:
> Hand-Holding (MAIN COMPLAINT): I give Duet any task, and it always needs something from me, rather its as simple as a "Yes" on a task i already told it to do, it WILL NOT merge PRs, it can't even merge a PR into my development branch. Which is extremely annoying when trying to have an agent ship real work (i get not shipping straight to a master branch, but even then if I wish to do that, it should..)
> Responses: Every time I ask a simple question, ask it to get something done, it comes back with 3 bubbles I have to read through.
> Tasks/Main Chat: Sometimes it's hard to navigate where it is responding at, sometimes its in the task thread, sometimes it's in the channel, and sometimes it's in both

As always @gabemulley I hope you see this and keep shipping the work on Duet, I see this becoming a main part of my workflow in the next few months.

note_tweet.text:
You are my lead Grok Bot. Tonight you run my backlog the way SpaceXAI engineer Lauren Tan runs her agents with pstack, her open source skill set: "i'm going to bed. land the stack even if ci flakes." My backlog is at the end.

READ FIRST
From the cursor/plugins repo on GitHub (github dot com slash cursor slash plugins, written out so X can't shorten it), folder pstack/skills, commit c742dd6, read: poteto-mode, sharpen, swarm, tdd, arena, show-me-your-work, ketchup. They were written for coding agents: skip any step that needs a tool you don't have, and tell me which.

1. SHARPEN
Do what sharpen does: make my ask deeper, not bigger. Add what a top professional would do that I didn't ask for, and name the raw material they'd start from. Ask me at most 4 questions, only ones that change the plan. Then write the pass condition: a check that can actually fail and that you can run (tests exit 0, a script, a diff that stays inside the plan). Save both to /workspace/run/plan.md. No Bot starts until I answer.

2. SWARM
Cut the backlog into slices that share data, not decisions. Propose one focused Bot per slice (6 by default, never more than 15): name, slice, its own pass check, the files it may touch. Wait for my OK before you create them. Slices run in parallel, every Bot reports back to you, and you merge it all into one report. Every Bot reply counts toward usage, so keep messages short and only between Bots that need each other.

3. TDD
Every Bot writes the failing test first, runs it and shows it fail, then writes the fix and shows it pass. No test, no fix. If CI flakes, retry once, then mark it flaky and move on. At most 3 rounds per slice; if a slice still fails, send back only that slice.

4. ARENA
For the 1 to 3 hardest parts (you pick, tell me which), run several attempts at the same part in parallel, each with a different approach, 3 by default. Prove every attempt with its tests, then take the best part of each into one version. Keep the losing attempts on their own branches, don't delete them.

5. SHOW ME YOUR WORK
Every Bot logs each decision to /workspace/run/decisions.tsv: time, Bot, decision, why, evidence, can it be undone. One line each, plain words. I will commit this file and read it over coffee.

6. ASK FIRST
Do everything that can be undone on your own. Wake me only for what can't be undone: merging to main, migrations, deleting data or Bots, spending money, anything public or sent to people. Before we start, list the Custom Rules I should add in Settings, General, Auto-review so Grok Bot enforces this too.

7. 8:00
Make one routine for 8:00 tomorrow: a ketchup in under 100 plain words (what landed, what was dropped and why), the merged swarm report, then each decision waiting on me with your pick, the evidence and the risk. Write "unknown" for anything you don't know.

MY BACKLOG
[paste the backlog you've been dodging all week]

note_tweet.text:
i asked claude about the possibility of using an ngrok setup.  not sure if this is possible or blocked on the bot computer but here is what i was told

Yes, an ngrok (or similar tunnel) setup is a reasonable workaround and should work.
Why it should work
The Nov 6 change is intentional. Cursor/Grok Bot support confirmed the browser process is now blocked from connecting to loopback (127.0.0.1 / localhost) except for the built-in egress proxy on port 8791. This is a security measure so that any page open in the bot’s browser can’t reach services running on the bot computer itself. The shell is unaffected, which is why curl still works.
Public sites continue to load normally in the browser. An ngrok (or Cloudflare Tunnel / cloudflared) URL is just a normal public HTTPS address, so the browser can open it. Traffic goes out to ngrok’s servers and is forwarded back to the local port on the bot computer.
Practical setup sketch
1On the bot computer (via shell), install ngrok and authenticate with a free auth token.
2Run something like ngrok http 7080 (or whatever local forwarder / service port you were using).
3Have the bot open the public https://….ngrok-free.app URL in its browser instead of http://127.0.0.1:7080.
Cloudflare’s quick tunnels (cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:PORT) are a no-account alternative for short-lived use and are commonly recommended for similar “expose localhost to a remote agent” scenarios.
Caveats
•Free ngrok URLs are random and temporary; a paid plan (or Cloudflare with your own domain) gives stable hostnames.
•The service becomes publicly reachable. Protect it with auth on the app itself, or use ngrok’s basic auth / Cloudflare Access.
•Keep the tunnel process running (nohup, systemd user service, etc.).
•For your previous Tailscale + local port-forwarder setup to the home NAS, you can point the tunnel at the local forwarder port. Alternatively, run the tunnel from the NAS side if that is cleaner.
Shell-based access (curl, CLIs, etc.) remains the simplest path when you don’t need the browser UI. Enterprise plans have official private-network options (Team Setup Scripts, Network Controls, etc.), but those are not available on personal plans.
If you try it and hit a specific snag (ngrok install, persistent service, auth, etc.), the details will help narrow it down.

note_tweet.text:
I asked Grok itself whether adding an extra $5 in usage credits would be worth it, and here’s what it told me:

An extra $5 in usage credits (Extra Usage Credits / Additional Usage) won’t get you very far if you’re using Grok Bot, even with light usage.

Why those credits run out so quickly

* Higher usage costs: Extra credits kick in once you’ve exhausted your included weekly allowance, and they’re charged at standard pay-as-you-go rates, which are higher than the effective rates included in your subscription. Agentic tasks in Grok Bot (tool calls, computer use, multi-step workflows, and long context windows) require significantly more compute than regular chat interactions.

* Real-world reports: Some users, even on the Ultra plan, have reported burning through $5 in credits after just two messages to the bot. Others have reportedly spent hundreds of dollars in a single day or over just a few days with heavier usage.

* No fixed conversion rate: xAI doesn’t publish a fixed equivalent like “$5 = X tasks or Y hours.” Actual consumption depends on token usage, the model the bot uses, context length, whether images or PDFs are involved, group chats that trigger multiple bots, automated routines, and other factors.
